newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sees NATO compromise at Clinton summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sees NATO compromise at Clinton summit.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, declaring himself fighting fit again on Russia's annual celebration of military might, hit out at NATO's expansion plans and said he expected Bill Clinton to compromise at a summit next month.

"We are firm in our position. We are opposed to NATO enlargement. Our task now is to stall it as long as possible and not allow the renewal of confrontation," Yeltsin said after a short ceremony marking Russia's Defenders of the Fatherland Day.

"We have agreed to look for a compromise and I think we will find this compromise at the summit we are holding with President Clinton on March 20-21 in Helsinki," he told reporters on his first public appearance since he caught pneumonia at New Year.
On Friday, Yeltsin, 66, discussed plans for the summit with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. Albright said she made "important progress" but much work was still needed.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov kept up his anti-NATO rhetoric, warning in a speech to veterans that the army was heading for financial ruin and that the West might therefore try to place Russia's nuclear arsenal under United Nations control.
"NATO is making every effort to deprive Russia of its strategic nuclear forces," Rodionov was quoted as saying.
Yeltsin said the army should not worry.
Declaring he was "still a fighter" and warning his opponents he was ready to "hit back", the president said: "I have fully recovered now. I just have to gain some strength."
He was feeling stronger after losing 26 kg (57 pounds) since the November heart bypass surgery which has kept him on the sidelines since his re-election last July.

With Yeltsin apparently getting back into his stride, the Helsinki summit may emerge as the climactic duet of an elaborate diplomatic round in which Western officials have been trying to overcome Moscow's bitter opposition to plans to allow former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe to join NATO.

"Knowing that pure Yeltsin style of solving problems in one go and in the most unexpected ways, this summit could get rid of the bitterest issues dividing Moscow and Washington," the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper wrote at the weekend.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was due to meet NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana in Brussels late on Sunday. Officials have imposed a virtual news blackout on the talks.
Western diplomats said Solana wanted to see how far Moscow was prepared to compromise following several NATO concessions.

It has offered to revise a 1990 treaty on the deployment of conventional forces and give Russia a say in NATO. The West has pledged not to base nuclear arms in new member states. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are the favourites for early entry.

Moscow, which sees NATO expansion as a threat and a domestic political embarrassment, has been holding out for a legally binding treaty laying down relations between NATO and Russia. The West wants to avoid a treaty needing parliamentary approval.
The government newspaper "Rossiiskaya Gazeta" conceded in a weekend editorial that Moscow could not halt NATO's expansion.

"Alas, the train has left and Russia is in no condition to give it the red light," commentator Vladimir Lapsky wrote. "The Russian government understands that and is basing its policy on finding an optimal accord with the West on the speed of this train, on what stops it makes and, especially, on its cargo."
The good atmosphere during Albright's visit, Lapsky added, "allows us to hope for a compromise that would suit everyone".
The government needs no reminding of the importance of being seen by voters to be defending Russia's interests.
Several thousand communists and nationalists marched through Moscow on Sunday under red banners accusing Yeltsin of wrecking the Soviet superpower and undermining the army.
